headline: The AI unwind won the week: the Nasdaq fell 4.5% while the Dow rose 0.7%, Brent settled near $110 on record attacks around Hormuz, and the scorecard says the oil and health care calls work while the AI chip calls do not.
summary: Thursday's pause did not hold. On Friday the Nasdaq fell 2.1% and the S&P 500 1.1%, CoreWeave fell 11.9% and the VIX jumped to 19.99, while energy and defense rose. For the week the S&P 500 lost 1.95%, the Nasdaq 4.48% and the Russell 2000 3.0%, but the Dow gained 0.67%. The 10 year yield fell 14.6 basis points to 5.097%, its biggest weekly drop since February, even as Brent settled at $109.86 after at least ten ships were attacked near Hormuz this week and Ukraine ended its energy truce. The JPM $310 put idea is dropped: its live quote pays only 4.9% a year, less than a 10 year Treasury. PFE is the only swing setup left, and nothing is confirmed.

regime.why: Money is leaving AI hardware, software and borrowers and moving to energy, defense, health care and the Dow, so the index hides a real split. Oil near $110 and December hike odds near 89% are the risks; falling Treasury yields are the cushion. Normal size only on breakouts that close over the pivot on 1.5x volume, and keep stops set over the weekend.

signals.title: The AI unwind resumes: the Nasdaq falls 2.1% Friday and 4.5% for the week as CoreWeave drops 11.9% and chip stocks fall for an eighth day, while the Dow ends the week up
signals.since_yesterday: Thursday's bounce failed. Friday closes: Nasdaq -2.14%, S&P 500 -1.09%, CoreWeave -11.9%, VIX 19.99; weekly Nasdaq -4.48% against Dow +0.67%.
signals.what_happened: On Oct 16 the Nasdaq fell 2.14% to 26,140.03, the S&P 500 1.09% to 7,659.44, the Dow 0.34% to 52,002.41 and the Russell 2000 1.7% to 2,721.37 (AP). For the week the S&P 500 lost 1.95%, the Nasdaq 4.48% and the Russell 3.0%, while the Dow gained 0.67% (AP, Stock Rover). The Philadelphia chip index fell about 2.5%, its eighth straight decline, and the selling spread to software and security, which lost about 7.7% on the week (TradingKey). By dashboard closes CoreWeave fell 11.9% to 61.39 on 2.8 times normal volume, AMD 6.0% to 528.75, HPE 6.0% to 55.13, Micron 5.6% to 878.84, Oracle 4.6% to 128.23, Broadcom 4.5% to 328.75, the TSMC ADR 2.3% to 412.61 and Nvidia 1.4% to 214.13. CoreWeave's five year default swaps passed 1,000 basis points this week, with an intraday record of 1,194.5 on Oct 15 per ICE, and its 2031 and 2032 bonds yielded about 16% (The Next Web, TradingNews). CNN's Fear and Greed index fell to 28. Friday was also monthly options expiration, and the VIX jumped from 16.46 to 19.99 (dashboard).
signals.so_what: The credit market is setting the price of AI now, not the order books. TSMC beat and raised two days ago and its stock still fell, because buyers are worried about who pays the bills. The borrowers (CoreWeave, Oracle) fall hardest, then the suppliers with the most to lose if spending pauses (memory, networking, chip equipment). Who gets paid: cash rich businesses that do not need the AI build out, plus energy and defense. What becomes scarce: willing lenders to AI builders; CoreWeave's swaps price a high chance of default even though analysts say no default is near. What would turn it: a refinancing that clears for an AI builder, or SK hynix (Oct 28) showing memory demand is still tight. Until then rallies in chips are for selling, not chasing. We mark CoreWeave, Oracle and Micron as hurt; Nvidia and TSMC are left out because their own results have not changed, only their prices.
signals.for_you: Swing: no chip or software setups, and none should be forced. Long term: AMD (528.75, zone 467.73 to 553.25), MRVL (227.83) and LITE (824.13) are still 'Buy zone now' on the numbers, but the group has fallen eight days in a row; if you add, use a small tranche or wait for the chip index to stop making lower lows. ALAB (up/down volume under 1.0), HPE (down more than 8% in a month), KEYS and SNPS slipped to 'Buy zone, wait for the chart'; AMAT, LRCX, CRDO and VIAV fell to Wait. Puts: avoid CRWV and ORCL. The HPE $55 scanner put on the scorecard is now right at the strike (55.13).

signals.title: Brent settles at $109.86, its highest since May, as attacks near Hormuz hit a record and Ukraine ends its energy truce; energy leads Friday
signals.since_yesterday: Brent rose 3.7% on Oct 16 and 4.9% on the week; WTI rose 10.4% on the week to $101.41. At least ten ships have been attacked near Hormuz since Oct 11, and a missile aimed at Yanbu was shot down on Oct 17.
signals.what_happened: Brent settled at $109.86 on Oct 16, up $3.94 or 3.7%, after touching $110 for the first time since May 19; WTI settled at $101.41, up 3.5% (Bloomberg via Rigzone, TokenPost). For the week Brent rose 4.9% and WTI 10.4%. A monitoring agency counted at least ten vessels attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz since Sunday Oct 11, a record pace, and Iran's Revolutionary Guards said an oil tanker caught fire after hitting a mine (CBS). On Oct 17 the Saudi led coalition said it intercepted a ballistic missile aimed at Yanbu, the Red Sea port Saudi Arabia uses to export without passing Hormuz, plus two cruise missiles and three drones; missiles also hit Aden's airport on Oct 16 (TRT, Al Jazeera). Tehran denied a role in Houthi attacks and offered to mediate. In Europe, Zelenskyy said 'we're done' with the energy truce after a Ukrainian strike set fire to Rosneft's Ryazan refinery, about 5% of Russia's refining (PBS). Energy was the best S&P 500 sector Friday, up about 2.5%, with six of 11 sectors higher (TradingKey). By dashboard closes EOG rose 3.5% to 158.01 on 1.75x normal volume, COP 3.4% to 146.51 on 1.16x, CVX 2.6% to 224.99 on 1.02x, XOM 2.5% to 178.98 on 0.97x and PSX 1.4% to 293.17 on 0.91x. DAL fell 3.5% to 75.37.
signals.so_what: The war has moved to the routes that were supposed to be the backup. Yanbu matters because it is Saudi Arabia's way around Hormuz; if it is hit, there is no detour left. Who pays: airlines, truckers and anyone buying diesel, and the Fed's inflation fight, which is why December hike odds sit near 89% even as Treasury yields fell. Who gets paid: US producers and refiners, whose crude does not pass Hormuz. Second order: high oil plus a hiking Fed is the mix that slowed the economy in 1990. What would make this wrong: Iran's mediation offer turning into a real ceasefire, which could take $10 or more off Brent quickly.
signals.for_you: Swing: EOG closed at 158.01, above its old 154.48 pivot on 1.75x normal volume, which meets the volume rule, but it is no longer on Setups and is already 2.3% past the pivot; if you are in from the Oct 14 call, the dashboard stop is 147.98. COP closed well over 141.91 but on only 1.16x, so it is still 'weak, wait'. Keep stops set this weekend: a ceasefire headline could gap oil names down. Puts: no energy put idea; SLB (49.50) and EQT (54.30) are 'Accumulate on pullback', not buys. Long term: avoid airlines (DAL fell to Wait).

signals.title: Defense rallies on a down day: Lockheed, RTX and Northrop rise about 4% on heavy volume
signals.what_happened: While the S&P 500 fell 1.1% on Oct 16, NOC rose 4.0% to 519.86, LMT 3.7% to 552.09 on 1.44x normal volume, RTX 3.7% to 193.92 on 1.87x, LHX 3.3% to 248.51 on 2.06x and GD 2.1% to 344.23 (dashboard). Coverage tied RTX's move to its recent awards, including a Navy SM-6 deal worth up to $24.4 billion and the SM-3 Block IB deal worth up to $6.3 billion. No single new contract explains the whole group; the timing matches the Gulf escalation.
signals.so_what: When a war spreads to new targets, missiles and interceptors get used faster than they are made, and the money follows to the few companies that build them. That is a chokepoint. The catch: the Pentagon is on a stopgap budget through Dec 11, so new programs cannot start yet. The rally is on volume, which is a better sign than price alone, but the dashboard's up/down volume for LMT (0.93) and RTX (0.74) is still under 1.0, so sellers have had the upper hand over recent weeks.
signals.for_you: Long term: LMT (552.09, zone 542.34 to 558.20) and RTX (193.92, zone 188.22 to 206.06) both moved to 'Buy zone, wait for the chart'. The check that fails is up/down volume under 1.0; two or three more up days on volume would fix it. No swing setup. Puts: none yet; wait for 'Buy zone now'.

signals.title: Cybersecurity breaks: Okta falls 10.2% and Palo Alto 7.6% after Bernstein downgrades and new AI rivals
signals.what_happened: By dashboard closes on Oct 16, OKTA fell 10.2% to 187.26 on 1.94x normal volume, S 7.7% to 21.58, PANW 7.6% to 342.00, CRWD 7.0% to 227.39, FTNT 7.0% to 169.13, NET 6.3% to 296.30 and ZS 5.9% to 207.38. Bernstein moved Okta, Palo Alto and SentinelOne to Market Perform, saying a near 100% rally since early 2026 had pushed prices to or above fair value, and reports of a rival security product from Perplexity added to the selling (Arabian Post). On Oct 14 a report that OpenAI plans to buy a security startup had already hit the group (24/7 Wall St.). CrowdStrike and Palo Alto are now more than 13% below their Oct 6 records (Motley Fool, Oct 17).
signals.so_what: Security spending is still rising, so this is about price and competition, not demand. Two things changed: the AI labs are moving into security themselves, and a group that doubled in a year had no cushion when growth stocks sold off. The platforms with the most customers (CrowdStrike, Palo Alto) are best placed to survive a price war; single product companies are more at risk. Watch whether any of them cut guidance in the coming reports; until then this is a valuation reset.
signals.for_you: No swing setups. Long term: CHKP (137.87, zone 129.17 to 147.11) held up, down only 0.2%, and is still 'Buy zone now'. FTNT is in its zone but now 'Buy zone, wait for the chart' (up/down 0.77). ZS (207.38) and S (21.58) are still above their zones ('Accumulate on pullback'); ZS's zone top is 197.74. Do not buy the drop in OKTA or PANW: both are rated Wait.

signals.title: Friday earnings: Travelers posts an 86.8% combined ratio and jumps on volume; Truist beats on adjusted profit and sells consumer lending units
signals.what_happened: Travelers reported Q3 core income of $9.18 a share ($1.947 billion) and net income of $9.04 a share, with a combined ratio of 86.8% and an underlying combined ratio of 84.1%, helped by $234 million of favorable reserve releases (8-K). TRV rose 1.5% to 389.54 on 2.23x normal volume (dashboard) and showed up on your MT Breakout Trigger scan at 11:25am. Truist reported diluted EPS of $0.56 and adjusted EPS of $1.16, up 12% from a year ago; it is selling its Retail Auto Credit business, plans to sell LightStream, returned $1.8 billion to shareholders, and posted its best wealth management quarter (8-K, Investing.com). Truist shares were down 0.9% premarket at $46.15; the close was not found.
signals.so_what: Insurers are pricing risk well: an 84.1% underlying ratio means about 16 cents of profit on each premium dollar before investment income. Truist exiting car loans and unsecured personal loans says a large regional bank would rather hold capital than consumer credit late in the cycle. That fits the cycle read: lenders are getting pickier, and the weakest borrowers feel it first.
signals.for_you: TRV has no dashboard verdict, so it is research only; a scanner hit with no verdict is not a buy. TFC is not on the dashboard. Bank puts: see the JPM decision below; the idea is dropped on premium, not on the bank's results.

signals.title: Health care holds its gains as the rotation spreads to energy and defense; MDT, DXCM, PODD and ZBH move into 'Buy zone now', and the FDA approves a presbyopia drop
signals.since_yesterday: Health care went flat on Friday instead of leading, which pulled MDT back into its buy zone; Viatris said the FDA approved Ryzumvi for presbyopia on Oct 16.
signals.what_happened: The big health care ETF was flat at midday on Oct 16 (Yahoo) as energy led. By dashboard closes LLY rose 0.4% to 1,257.03, ABBV 0.7% to 285.42 and PFE 0.5% to 29.58, while GILD fell 0.7% to 156.19, MDT 0.7% to 94.75 and UNH 1.3% to 401.43. The pause moved MDT (94.75), DXCM (86.04), PODD (141.10) and ZBH (94.98) to 'Buy zone now', while REGN (790.74) and ZTS (79.38) slipped to 'Buy zone, wait for the chart' because up/down volume fell under 1.0. Separately, Viatris said the FDA approved Ryzumvi (phentolamine 0.75% eye drops) for presbyopia, one day before its Oct 17 goal date; Viatris holds US rights under a license from Opus Genetics, and the approval rests on the VEGA-2 and VEGA-3 trials.
signals.so_what: The rotation into health care is not reversing; it is resting while money finds the next place to hide (energy and defense). That is the healthy kind of pause, because prices held. On presbyopia: Ryzumvi works by shrinking the pupil, the same pinhole idea as earlier drops, which had slow uptake, so expect a modest launch. It matters more for the small developer than for Viatris.
signals.for_you: Long term: MDT (94.75, zone 84.33 to 93.09), DXCM (86.04), PODD (141.10, zone 136.22 to 191.33) and ZBH (94.98) are 'Buy zone now'; a small tranche fits. Abbott reports Oct 21 before the open and ABT (104.89) is above its 98.39 to 100.45 zone, so wait. Swing: PFE is the only setup (see Actions). Clinically, Ryzumvi is a new near vision option to know about; it is not a dashboard name.

signals.title: World check: the KOSPI's worst week since 2008, Brazil's runoff is a tie in polls but not in betting, and China's GDP lands Sunday night
signals.what_happened: South Korea's KOSPI rose 2.05% to 5,668.06 on Oct 16 but lost 14.46% for the week, its biggest weekly drop since October 2008 (TradingKey); Samsung closed at 215,500 won and SK hynix at 1,272,000 won. In New York EWY fell 3.7% to 150.44 on Friday (dashboard). The Bank of Korea, at 3.00%, decides on Oct 22. In Brazil, a Futura/100% Cidades poll released Oct 16 has Flavio Bolsonaro at 50.8% of valid votes to Lula's 49.2%, a technical tie inside its 2.2 point margin; an eleven pollster average is 51.6% to 48.4%, while Polymarket (77%) and Kalshi (78%) favored Bolsonaro as of Oct 16 (Rio Times). EWZ rose 0.6% to 41.83 on 1.58x volume and NU fell 1.2% to 14.56. China publishes Q3 GDP at 02:00 GMT on Oct 19 (7pm Pacific on Sunday Oct 18); a Reuters poll expects 4.4%, below the 4.5% to 5% target. China's September rare earth exports rose 6.7% from a year ago to 4,269.8 tonnes, though they are still down 9.6% for the year (SMM).
signals.so_what: Korea is where the AI memory trade is most crowded, and a 14% week is forced selling, not a calm repricing. If SK hynix (Oct 28) shows demand is still tight, Korea could bounce hard; if not, there is more to go. In Brazil, the betting markets are far more sure than the polls, which means a Lula win would be the bigger surprise and the bigger move. China's number matters for copper and for US companies selling there.
signals.for_you: No action this weekend. Korea: no MU or memory swings; avoid Korean bank ADRs before Oct 22. Brazil: NU (14.56, zone 14.03 to 15.08) is 'Buy zone now', but wait until after the Oct 25 runoff before buying or selling puts. If you hold the EWZ $37 scanner put, its cushion is 13.1%.

signals.title: Scorecard: how the calls did
signals.what_happened: From site/data/scorecard.json (calls since Oct 6, graded through Oct 16). Swing: 20 calls, 3 finished, 1 win (ABBV +2R), 2 losses (ANET and ZBRA, -1R each), average 0.0R; 11 open, 6 waiting. The open energy swings are all positive: XOM +1.28R, CVX +0.87R, COP +0.75R, EOG +0.54R, PSX +0.06R. Open health swings are near flat: PFE +0.28R, GILD +0.24R, WST +0.03R, BDX -0.08R. Puts: 8 open, none finished, so no premium has been kept or lost yet. Three scanner puts are close to their strikes: HPE $55 (stock 55.13), DAL $75 (75.37) and BHP $82.50 (83.29). The brief's own puts have more room: PFE $27 (9.6% cushion), JPM $310 (9.6%), C $120 (3.6%). Long term buys: beat the S&P 500 over 5 days in 33 of 75 graded calls (44%), an average of 2.87 points behind. The Oct 9 batch did worst (5 of 18, 7.84 points behind), led by chip equipment and optics: OUST -26.78, COHR -23.53, TER -17.32, AMAT -17.31, LRCX -15.25. The best were health care and financials: CVS +9.17, ZTS +8.08, MA +7.05, MDT +6.94, PGR +5.25. Signals: right in 31 of 55 graded calls (56%), 0.65 points ahead of the S&P 500 on average. Bullish energy signals went 7 for 7 (7.58 points ahead on average) and bullish health signals 9 for 9 (4.39 ahead). Bullish AI chip and power signals went 0 for 9 (MRVL, AVGO, TSM, AMD, MU, CEG, CCJ, GEV, MP; 8.35 points behind on average). Bearish calls on energy (0 for 5) and health (0 for 4) were also all wrong.
signals.so_what: What works: following the money into oil and health care while it is moving there. What does not: calling AI hardware bullish because the long term story is good while the chart and the credit market say no. The bearish calls against energy and health failed for the same reason in reverse: we fought the flow. Honest caveat: every group here has fewer than 20 finished calls and the record covers only about two weeks of one unusual market, so none of this is proof. It is a reason to tighten one rule, not to throw out the method.
signals.for_you: Rule change to consider: no bullish signal or long term buy call on a chip or AI hardware name while the chip index is below its 50 day average, and no bearish call on a sector that is leading the market unless its own news turned. If you hold swings, the energy group is where the open profits are; protect them with the dashboard stops. If you sold puts like the HPE, DAL or BHP scanner picks, decide before Monday's open whether you would take the shares; roll only for a net credit and only on 'Buy zone now' names (none of the three is).

cycle.quadrant_why: Inflation: September CPI 3.7% and PPI 6.3% (released Oct 14 and 15), and Brent settled at $109.86 on Oct 16, up 4.9% on the week. Growth: jobless claims 199,000 (week to Oct 10) and retail sales up 0.8%, but only 0.2% without gas stations. Jobs hold while real spending is flat, so this is still rising inflation with steady but slowing growth.
cycle.short_term_debt_cycle: Late. The Fed is at 3.75% to 4.00% after a September hike. October hike odds are about 15% (CME), but December odds were reported near 89% on Oct 16. The 10 year fell 14.6 basis points this week to 5.097% as money hid in Treasuries. Credit is tightening for the weakest borrowers: CoreWeave's default swaps passed 1,000 basis points, and Truist is selling its car loan and personal loan units. Late in the cycle, lenders pull back first from the riskiest borrowers, and that is what this week showed.
cycle.long_term_debt_cycle: Late. Government debt is high, long rates are near 5.1%, and part of the AI build out runs on borrowed money that lenders now price as risky. With inflation at 3.7% and oil near $110, the Fed has little room to rescue markets with cuts.
cycle.big_cycle: Four of five forces are active, and the external order force got stronger this week. Debt and money: hot inflation, possible December hike, AI credit stress. External order: a record pace of ship attacks near Hormuz, a missile aimed at Saudi Arabia's Yanbu bypass port, and the end of Ukraine's energy truce. Internal order: fuel prices before the Nov 3 midterms. Technology: AI demand is real, but the market is now questioning who pays for it.
tailwinds: The 10 year yield fell 14.6 basis points this week to 5.097%, its biggest weekly drop since February.
Jobs are solid: claims at 199,000, the fifth week under 200,000.
Rotation, not panic: the Dow rose 0.67% for the week while the Nasdaq fell 4.48%.
headwinds: Brent at $109.86, its highest since May, with the attacks moving to the routes around Hormuz.
December hike odds near 89%: oil keeps the Fed hawkish even as growth slows.
Credit stress in AI borrowers (CoreWeave swaps above 1,000 basis points) and an eighth straight drop in chip stocks.

history.when: 1990 to 1991, the Gulf War oil shock
history.what: After Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990, crude nearly doubled from about $20 to about $40 a barrel. With the Fed already squeezing inflation and credit tight, the US slipped into a recession that began in July 1990.
history.lesson: An oil shock on top of tight money can tip a slowing economy into recession. Energy producers did well; consumers, airlines and lenders did not.

source.title: The Gulf War recession, 1990 to 1991 (TrendSpider Learning Center)

history.what: Telecom companies raised about $1.6 trillion, including about $600 billion of bonds, to build fiber networks; by late 2002 about 23 telecom companies had gone bankrupt.
history.lesson: In a debt funded build out, demand can be real and the borrowers can still fail. The suppliers with cash survived; the leveraged builders did not.

source.title: AI debt bubble: dot com and telecom lessons (IBTimes)

cycle.differences: The 1990 oil shock replaces 1998 today, because the new facts are oil near $110 and attacks moving to Saudi Arabia's bypass routes, not a narrow credit scare. What is different: in 1990 the Fed could cut once the recession started; today inflation is 3.7% and the next move priced is a hike, so the cushion is smaller. What still rhymes with 2000 to 2002: the stress sits with the AI borrowers, not the cash rich chokepoint suppliers.
cycle.for_you: Swing: favor what is working and has volume (energy, some health care), keep stops set over the weekend, and skip chips. Puts: VIX near 20 makes premiums richer, but only sell where you want the shares and the yield beats Treasuries; today nothing on the list does. Long term: buy in small tranches only where the verdict is 'Buy zone now', and prefer cash rich health care and financials over borrowers.
